newsitem.title: KENYA: Rights groups row over Rwanda genocide suspect.
newsitem.headline: Rights groups row over Rwanda genocide suspect.

text.p: A row between human rights groups over how they handled the arrest of a Rwandan Hutu accused of rape, sexual mutilation and having a leading role in the 1994 genocide raises questions about their methods of operating.
London-based Amnesty International (AI) rejects the accusations it failed through ignorance in the case of Joseph Ruyenzi.
African Rights says the case proves such agencies must closely investigate cases before publicising them.

"Even if we had been wrong in this case, which we were not, it would not undermine our credibility. We were responsible in terms of actions provided," Firoze Manji, Amnesty's programme director for Africa, told Reuters from London on Monday night.

"In our assessment, many of the cases recently highlighted by AI are characterised by an absence of thorough, independent investigation; a lack of evidence to support sweeping allegations; and the invariable use of a poorly researched case to support allegations of systematic policies of abuse," African Rights said in a report on the Ruyenzi case issued last week.
It titled the report "Prisoner Without a Conscience", a parody of Amnesty's successful "Prisoner of Conscience" campaigns.

On March 30 last year Ruyenzi, then a newsreader at state Radio Rwanda, was arrested and accused of raping and sexually mutilating Donatilla Mujawimana during the genocide in 1994 in which hardline Hutus killed an estimated 800,000 Tutsis and moderate Hutus. He says he is innocent.

Amnesty says its information was that he was not charged, so, as is usual in such circumstances, it called on its members through an "urgent action" notice to call for his release unless he was charged with a criminal offence.
It issued three "urgent action" notices concerning Ruyenzi.

African Rights says that in its eight-month investigation it found no irregularities with Ruyenzi's arrest and charging and accuses Amnesty of moulding his case with little information to set off a high-profile campaign suggesting he was persecuted.

"The message which Amnesty members received was that in Rwanda freedom of speech is not tolerated, arbitrary arrest and detention is a common fate for the critical journalist and torture is part of prison culture," African Rights said.
Reporters Sans Frontieres, which campaigns for journalists' rights, first reported fears for Ruyenzi's safety and warned about an eventual operation to purify ethnically Rwanda's state-owned media.
It told African Rights it had later interviewed Ruyenzi, his accusors and other witnesses and called for a deeper inquiry but gave him $200 to subsidise his needs in detention.

"Our findings highlight the consequences of a lack of thorough research, raising fundamental questions about the criteria by which some international human rights organisations define abuses," African Rights said.
"They demonstrate the urgent need for a discussion about the institutional practices of organisations concerned," it said.

"We would stress it is not up to Amnesty to make judgments on the guilt or otherwise...but due process has to be followed. We believe we acted quite correctly," said Manji, adding its Africa section alone issued scores of urgent alerts each month.
In contrast to Amnesty's position of refusing to judge guilt or innocence, African Rights says Ruyenzi was a key instigator of the genocide and allegedly raped and mutilated Mujawimana.

"This report has only documented a fraction of his crimes. We hope it will be used by the Rwandese government to broaden its own investigation," says African Rights, which arranged for a doctor to examine Mujawimana to confirm her rape accusations.
"We hope the way in which the material was put in the public domain does not give grounds for a defence claim due process was not followed and he cannot receive a fair trial," Manji said.
